Definition: Whether and how the central bank participates in payment system governance beyond its regulatory oversight role, including board representation, operational management, technical standard-setting, or direct system operation.
Comments: The Central Bank of Tunisia (BCT) directly operates core payment infrastructure: Elyssa-RTGS (RTGS) with published adhesion conditions/rules and participant obligations. Interbank clearing is supported by SIBTEL (a private company created by BCT and banks), indicating direct central bank involvement in governance and operation of key systems.
revision_notes: Confirmed. Primary BCT sources (Note 2022-05 on Elyssa-RTGS adhesion conditions, the official BCT payment systems webpage, and Circular 2024-005 on payment/settlement system governance) verify that BCT directly owns, operates and supervises the Elyssa-RTGS/SGMT infrastructure, consistent with the 'Direct Operation' code (5), the maximum on the 0-5 scale. The score is unchanged from the original but rests on strong, current, authoritative primary-source evidence directly on point, so it stands as confirmed rather than a promotion requiring escalation. The originally cited ubmonline.org source could not be retrieved (timeout) and has been replaced with verified BCT primary sources.
revised_comments: The Central Bank of Tunisia (BCT) directly owns, operates and supervises core national payment infrastructure, including the Elyssa-RTGS real-time gross settlement system and the SGMT gross settlement system, under powers granted by Law No. 2016-35. BCT publishes participant adhesion conditions for Elyssa-RTGS itself and, through circulars such as Circular No. 2024-005, sets governance requirements for payment and securities settlement system operators generally, while acting as owner, supervisor, manager and an ordinary participant of the RTGS system.

Definition: Whether legal or regulatory requirements obligate payment service providers to notify users, regulators, and/or data protection authorities about payment data breaches, cybersecurity incidents, or unauthorized access within specified timeframes.
Comments: Breach notification obligations exist in general privacy/cyber frameworks: sources describe notification to authorities (INPDP/public prosecutor) for certain incidents, and Decree-Law 2023-17 is referenced as mandating cyber-attack notification to ANCS for telecom processing contexts; not clearly tailored to payment systems, but mandatory obligations exist.
revision_notes: Confirmed. Verified via DLA Piper's dedicated breach-notification summary and the primary text of Decree-Law No. 2023-17 (11 March 2023), which mandates notification to the National Cybersecurity Agency (ANCS) following a cyberattack for entities processing personal data via telecommunications networks (a category encompassing payment service providers), with financial penalties (Art. 25) for non-compliance. This supports the 'Mandatory' code (3) on the 0-3 scale. The originally cited accessnow.org source discussed digitisation privacy risks generally but did not itself evidence a breach-notification rule; it has been replaced with the primary Decree-Law text and DLA Piper's breach-notification page.
revised_comments: Tunisia's Decree-Law No. 2023-17 of 11 March 2023 on cybersecurity requires entities engaged in automated processing of personal data via telecommunications networks, a category that includes payment service providers, to notify the National Cybersecurity Agency (ANCS) in the event of a cyberattack, with financial penalties for non-compliance. The National Authority for Protection of Personal Data (INPDP) separately refers detected data protection offences to the public prosecutor. Together these establish a mandatory breach and incident notification regime, albeit one grounded in general cybersecurity and data protection law rather than payment-specific regulation.

Definition: Whether national data protection or privacy legislation exists and explicitly covers payment transaction data, including provisions on data collection, storage, sharing, retention, and user rights over their payment data.
Comments: Tunisia has a general data protection law (Organic Law 2004-63) and discussion of GDPR-aligned updates (e.g., draft 2019-36) but no payment-system-specific privacy regime was evidenced in the sources consulted; score reflects existence of general privacy framework.
revision_notes: Confirmed. Both cited sources verify Organic Law 2004-63 as a general data protection framework covering all personal data processing (automated and non-automated), with no payment-specific data provisions identified, supporting the 'General Data Protection Legislation' code (2) on the 0-3 scale.
revised_comments: Tunisia's Organic Law No. 2004-63 of 27 July 2004 on the Protection of Personal Data establishes a general data protection framework applying to all automated and non-automated processing of personal data by natural or legal persons, without payment-specific provisions. The law is implemented through Decree 2007-3003 (establishing the National Authority for Personal Data Protection, INPDP) and Decree 2007-3004 (governing declaration and authorisation of data processing), and its constitutional basis has been reaffirmed in the 2014 and 2022 constitutions. No dedicated legislative provisions addressing payment transaction data specifically have been identified.

Definition: Whether payment system governance explicitly includes mechanisms to ensure inclusivity and represent interests of vulnerable populations, including provisions for input from all participant types, consumer representatives, small providers, or explicit financial inclusion mandates in governance documents.
Comments: Tunisia adopted a National Financial Inclusion Strategy (NFIS) 2018–2022 (validated by the Ministerial Council) that includes digital finance/digital payments as an inclusion lever; evidence indicates pro-inclusion orientation but no clear, binding payment-system pro-poor governance mechanisms identified beyond the strategy framework.
revision_notes: Confirmed. Original NFIS sources verified, and an additional primary source was located (BCT Circular 2020-11 on domestic mobile payment services, Article 18) linking mobile payment-service pricing/governance explicitly to the national financial inclusion and cash-reduction strategy. No explicit pro-poor governance structures (e.g., reserved board seats, formal consumer representation) were found, so the evidence supports 'Partial' (2) rather than 'Yes' (3) on the 0-3 scale.
revised_comments: Tunisia's National Financial Inclusion Strategy (NFIS), validated by the Select Ministerial Council in June 2018 and covering 2018-2022, identifies digital finance among its priority axes and has been supported through technical assistance from the French Development Agency, Horus Development Finance and ADA. BCT Circular No. 2020-11 governing domestic mobile payment services requires that pricing approaches for mobile payment services have regard to the national strategy for financial inclusion and cash reduction. No formal payment-system governance mechanisms have been identified, however, such as reserved board seats for consumer or small-provider representatives or a standing consumer advisory body.

Definition: Whether the scheme rules governing payment system participation, pricing structure, technical requirements, security standards, and conduct are publicly accessible via website, public repository, or on request. Transparency indicator.
Comments: Scheme/system rules are publicly accessible: BCT publishes Elyssa-RTGS adhesion conditions/rules (operational requirements and participant obligations) online; media also references and links to these publicly available conditions.
revision_notes: Confirmed. The BCT's own published Note 2022-05 (the full adhesion conditions/rules for Elyssa-RTGS) and the public BCT webpage on payment systems verify full public availability of scheme rules, supporting 'Yes - Fully Public' (3), the maximum code on the 0-3 scale. This is confirmed on strong primary-source evidence (the regulator's own publicly hosted rules document), not a new promotion, so it is not flagged for further review.
revised_comments: The Central Bank of Tunisia (BCT) publishes the adhesion conditions and operating rules for its Elyssa-RTGS real-time settlement system online (Note No. 2022-05 of 15 February 2022), covering requirements for direct and indirect participants and external systems, and these have been reported on and linked to by Tunisian business media. BCT also maintains a public webpage describing the SGMT/Elyssa-RTGS settlement system and the monetics clearing system, setting out participation, monitoring and administration arrangements.
